summary: Iterate finite-information operators from the nowhere-defined function to obtain an actual computable least solution.
abstract: A recursive definition may describe a value in terms of other values whose computations have not yet finished. When a rule can use only finitely many successful observations of an input partial function, start by giving it no answers and repeatedly collect what those observations justify. Each round retains earlier answers. Their union solves the recursive equation, is contained in every other solution, and is computed by one ordinary program that searches all finite rounds. That program has a primitive-recursive compiler from an index for the rule family. Simple equations show that the least solution may be total, partial, or one among many solutions. This is Kleene’s first recursion theorem; its leastness conclusion differs from finding a program whose behavior agrees with an index transformation.
